item.title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
item.description:
The U.S., Denmark and Greenland formally signed President Donald Trump’s new Greenland security agreement on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly Tuesday, cementing permanent U.S. military rights on the strategically vital Arctic island after months of negotiations over Trump’s push for greater American control. Trump, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark and Prime Minister Jens-Frederick Nielsen of Greenland met Tuesday morning for a trilateral signing ceremony, where the three parties praised each other's defense cooperation over the past 75 years, through World War II and the Cold War. In brief remarks, Trump praised both prime ministers for their efforts in making the deal happen, adding that, "we're going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship, and we look forward to it, and we'll be working very hard and very much in conjunction with each other."…

item.title: The House Freedom Caucus has to transform — it could preview the GOP's post-Trump era
item.description:
MS NOW White House Correspondent Akayla Gardner prepares to report from a street corner outside the White House grounds after being denied entry on Sept. 19, 2026. Graeme Sloan/Getty Images The president is going after the press again. item.title: Biden's Team Wanted War in the Middle East Without Owning It
item.description:
Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel's War in Gaza by Akbar Shahid Ahmed, W.W. Norton, 368 pages, $31.99 The U.S. government owns a share of what happened to Gaza. Through two administrations, Washington provided much of the money, weapons, and intelligence required to reconquer the Palestinian enclave, and U.S. troops were eventually deployed only a step removed from the front lines. Now the Trump administration has put its full diplomatic weight behind a "Board of Peace" aimed at reshaping Gaza forever, hoping to turn that board into a model for all global diplomacy. Akbar Shahid Ahmed has been one of the most well-sourced journalists documenting this process. His book Crossing the Red Line presents itself as a comprehensive account of the United States' involvement in the war. But it falls short of its potential.
